sections.heading: Pre-Historic ---- 3000 BCE
sections.content: Bhimbhetka has remained a landmark of generations of prehistoric art in India. It is believed that these paintings are twenty thousand to five hundred thousand years old. Bhimbetka lies south of Bhopal and is surrounded by the Vindhya ranges. Indian archaeologists date some of these paintings to the very early periods, including the Upper Palaeolithic period. But the statement has no reliable grounds. It can be dated rather to the Mesolithic. The Bhimbhetka Caves or rock shelters in Bhimbetka have ancient prehistoric paintings depicting the lives and times of people living in these caves. The scenes painted on the walls include animals around by them like wild buffalo, tigers, and rhinoceros. The scenes also depict activities from their lives like dance, religious rituals and childbirth. Other paintings depict the tools they used for cooking, hunting and other purposes. This makes the Bhimbetka group an archaeological treasure, an invaluable chronicle in the history of man and a World Heritage site. In Bhimbhtka, mineral and vegetable colours are primarily used. The colours used by the cave dwellers were prepared combining manganese, haematite, soft red stone and wooden coal. Sometimes the fat of animals and extracts of leaves were also used in the mixture. The colours have remained intact for many centuries due to the chemical reaction resulting from the oxide present on the surface of the rocks. The themes are taken from the everyday events depicting hunting, dancing, music, horse and elephant riders, animals fighting, honey collection, decoration of bodies, disguises and household scenes. Animals such as bisons, tigers, lions, wild boar, elephants, antelopes, dogs, lizards, crocodiles etc. have been abundantly depicted in some caves. The superimposition of paintings shows that the same surface was used by people of different times. Rock art, thus, gives tremendous clues to understand the life-style, entertainment or the mysticism prevalent in that era. The detailed concepts of animals from filled types to stick and x-ray types are found in abundance.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Monument- Khajuraho
sections.content: Known as the temple city of India, Khajuraho is known for its intricately carved, beautiful medieval temples. A symbol of India's glorious past, heritage and culture, the temples symbolize an immortal saga of Hindu art and culture in central India and are an outstanding image of the well developed Nagara style of temple architecture. Khajuraho was the historic capital of the Chandelas who built these temples from the ninth through the thirteenth centuries. Among the 85 original ones only 25 have survived the ravages of time. Around the temples are bands of fine work, portraying gods, goddesses, musicians, animals, etc. Erotic sculptures featuring apsaras and mithunas (couples) also dominate the themes portrayed here. shrine and four subsidiary shrines scattered around the landscape. The temples of Khajuraho are divided into three groups- the western,which is the largest group having temples dedicated to Shiva and Vishnu like Chitragupta Temple, Kandariya Mahadeo, Chausat Yogini Temple, Lakshmana Temple and Matangeswara Temple. The Eastern are the Jain temples including the temples of Pashvanath and the Adinatha which were built by the merchants and the Southern group, where the remains of the Vaidyanath Shiva temple has been exposed by the ASI (Archaeological survey of India). Khajuraho shows a highly evolved stage of Indian temple architecture. Most temples stand on a tall platform known as the Jagati. The elevation consists of three divisions: a pitha, the wall or jangha, and a roof or shikhara. Ornamentation is abundant on the basal storey in a series of mouldings. It depicts human activities, kirtimukhas and geometric designs. The wall section is divided into two or three sculptural sections including apsaras, mithunas and divine figures. As these figures rise upwards they add to the dramatic effect. The oldest of these temples, dating back to 900 CE is the Chaunsath Yogini temple, located southwest of the Shibsagar lake. Built of rough granite it is dedicated to the sixty four manifestations of the Mother Goddesses or the yoginis. This shrine is raised on a large platform in an open courtyard surrounded by miniature shrines for sixty four manifestations of the goddess. Kandariya Mahadeo temple is the largest in Khajuraho. It is considered to be the best representation of the nagara style of temples consisting of a garbhagriha or a sanctum, a circumambulatory path - pradakshinapatha, an antarala or the vestibule, ardhamandapa, mandapa and a mahamandapa. The sanctum enshrines a marble shivalingam. This mammoth structure stands 30 metres above the ground level. A rich variety of sculptures adorn the platform. They are sculptures of female figures in different poses engaged in writing letters, playing with a ball or applying makeup. The northern group has Vaishnava temples for the most part and the south eastern group consists of Jain temples. To the north of this temple is the Devi Jagadambi temple standing on the same platform as Kandariya Mahadeo. It is more delicately proportionate and the temple is decorated with some fine sculptures. Due to its smaller size, the sculptures are clearly visible. Further north is the sun temple, enshrining an image of the Sun God, on a chariot pulled by seven horses. To the extreme north of this, is the Vishwanath temple, built along the lines of the Kandariya Mahadeo temple. Inscriptions reveal that it was built by King Dhanga and that an emerald image of Shiva - Marakateswara was enshrined here. South west of this temple is the Parvati temple. The Lakshmana-Chaturbhuja temple stands on a platform which has a magnificent sculptural frieze of elephants and horse riders in a procession. There is also an embellishment of erotic sculptures. The Matangeswara temple enshrines Shiva, in the form of a highly polished gigantic Shivalingam. There is also a small Varaha temple with a gigantic monolithic image of a standing Varaha, the boar incarnation of Vishnu. The whole figure is carved in low relief. The main sanctum contains the image of Vaikunth Vishnu, bearing three heads representing his various incarnations. The eastern group has temples dedicated to Brahma. It is one of the smallest shrine with a single room having a shiv- linga protected by a huge pyramidal roof. Vamana and Javari are miniature versions of the western group of temples.

sections.heading: Adinath Temple, Parsvanath Temple, Ghantai Temple, Hanuman Temple and Brahma Temple
sections.content: Among the temples in the eastern zone, the ones worth mentioning are: Adinath Temple, Parsvanath Temple, Ghantai Temple, Hanuman Temple and Brahma Temple, which can be divided into two, the temples dedicated to the Jain pantheon and the temples dedicated to Hindu Gods and Goddesses. The Jain temples include the Parsavanath Temple dedicated to Parsavanath, the Jain Tirthankara. It is a well decorated and the largest Jain Temple. Adinath temple is dedicated to Adinath, a Jain Tirthankara. The sculpted figures of Yakshis are particularly famous here. Ghantai Temple is well known for the sculpture of a Jain goddess on a winged Garuda and for the sixteen dreams of Mahavira's mother. The temples in the southern zone has Dulah Deo temple dedicated to Lord Shiva and Chattarbhuj temple. The Dulah Deo Temple has been dedicated to Lord Shiva. It is supposed to have been constructed between 1100 CE and 1150. Inside the temple there is a vast Shivalingam. There is also an image of Lord Shiva at the very entrance of the temple.The architectural complex consists of the mandapa, where the shrine is placed, along with the mahamandapa and the ardhamandapa with no circumbulatory passage. There is also the cluster of the shikharas, both subsidiary and centralized. The Chaturbhuja temple consists of the shrine of Lord Vishnu, to whom this is dedicated. This temple has also been constructed in the 1100. The structure is more or less similar to the Dulah Dao Temple. The exotic sculptures add to the glamour and elegance of the place.

sections.heading: Wall paintings
sections.content: The city of Orchha was founded on the banks of Betwa in the sixteenth century by the Bundela chief Rudra Pratap, who became the first ruler of Orchha. In the early seventeenth century, Raja Jujhar Singh rebelled against the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, whose armies devastated the state and occupied Orchha from 1635 to 1641. The main historical monuments of Orchha are the Jehangir Mahal, Raj Mahal, Rai Praveen Mahal, Laxmi Narayan Temple and the Chaturbhuj Temple. The various palaces and temples built by the Bundela rulers retain much of their immaculate perfection. Of the succeeding rulers, the most notable was Raja Bir Singh who built the exquisite Jehangir Mahal, a tiered palace crowned with graceful Chhatries. Construction of the Raj Mahal was started by Rudra Pratap, and completed by one of his successors, Madhukar Shah. The Sheesh Mahal was built during the early 18th century, and was originally intended as an exclusive country retreat for the local king Udait Singh. It has two rectangular courtyards inside, the second, formerly used by the Bundela queens. Opulent royal quarters, raised balconies and interlocking walkways rise in symmetrical tiers on all four sides, crowned by domed pavilions and turrets. One can find the fragments of mirror-inlay and vibrant painting plastered over their walls and ceilings. Some of the friezes are still in remarkable condition. The Rai Praveen Mahal is a small, double-storeyed brick apartment built by Raja Indramani for his concubine in the mid seventeenth century. This building lies to the north of the Sheesh Mahal. The building, set amid the lawns of the Anand Mahal gardens, it has a main assembly hall on the ground floor, a private salon upstairs, and cool underground apartments. Entered through an ornate ceremonial gateway, the east-facing facade is covered with turquoise tiles. Two stone elephants flank the stairway, holding bells in their trunks to announce the arrival of the Raja. Three storeys of elegant hanging balconies, terraces, apartments and onion domes are piled around a central courtyard. This palace, however, is more airy and lighted since it has countless windows and pierced stone screens looking out over the skyline to the west, and a sea of treetops and ruined temples in the other direction.

sections.heading: Chaturbhuj Temple
sections.content: Ram Raja Mandir, a palace-turned-temple has a charming legend attached to it. King Madhukar Shah brought an idol of Lord Rama from Ayodhya to his capital following the dream visitation of God Ram to be installed later in a temple. When the idol proved impossible to move, the king recalled, too late, the deity's edict that the image would remain in the place where it was first installed. It is also the only temple in India where Ram is worshipped as a king. Chaturbhuj Temple was built upon a massive stone platform and reached by a steep flight of steps. The temple was specially constructed to enshrine the image of Ram which, however, remained in the Ram Raja Temple. Lotus emblems and symbols of religious importance provide the delicate exterior ornamentation. Laxminarayan Temple A flagstone path links the Laxminarayan Temple with the Ram Raja Temple. The style here is a mix of fort and temple architecture. The interiors contain the most exquisite of Orchha's wall paintings. On the walls and ceilings of three halls, these murals are vibrant compositions and cover a variety of spiritual and secular subjects.

sections.heading: Chanderi Fort
sections.content: The Chanderi fort is located in the small historical town of Chanderi in the Ashoknagar District of Madhya Pradesh. The fort is the most striking monument in this ancient town and it dates back to the Mughal Period. The Muslim rulers, especially the Malwa Sultans took a lot of initiative to construct the fortification walls of the fort. The mahals within the fort were built by the Bundela rajputs revealing various phases of building styles. Located on top of a hill, the fortified walls enclose the citadel and protect it from outsiders. The Fort is approached through three gates. The first and main gate is well known as the Khooni Darwaza. It has been so named because criminals were thrown from the battlements above and their bodies crashed to pieces below. Hawa Paur is the third and highest gate of the Chanderi fort. The remnants of the Chanderi Fort include the Hawa Mahal and the Nau Khanda Mahal. Both these buildings were built by the Bundela chiefs. There is yetanother gateway on the south western side of the fort referred to as the Khatti Ghatti which is about twenty five metres in height forming part of the outer defenses of the town. There is a Purana Madarsa which was used as a school in the sixteenth century. It has latticed screens with geometric designs set in closed arches and the walls are embellished with lotus medallions. There is a massive structure known as the Koshak Mahal which houses four identical palace buildings which are situated at the corner of a square courtyard. The plain exterior contrasts well with the ornate bay windows. The battisi baoli is the biggest step-well in Chanderi. Thirty-two broad steps from each side descend down to a square pool.

sections.heading: Lal Baag Palace, Indore
sections.content: Lal Baag palace is located in Indore. It is surrounded by gardens and was built between 1886 and 1921. It is one of the grandest ancestral monuments built by the Holkar dynasty. The rooms have been restored and furnished and much of the furniture and ornamentation is in the early Georgian style. Its Italian marble columns, grand chandeliers, rich Persian carpets, flying nymphs on the ceiling, Belgian stained glass windows, Greek mythological reliefs, Italian style wall paintings speak of its past glory.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Monument- Indore-Kanch Mandir
sections.content: As the name suggests, the full temple is made up of coloured glass. This Jain Temple was built by the Cotton King Sir Hukamchand in the early twentieth century. Inside this Jain temple thousands of mirrors adorn the walls, floor and ceilings, supplemented by brightly patterned ceramic tiles, Chinese lantern-type glass lamps and cut glass chandeliers. The use of glass beads and raised figures produces a pleasing three-dimentional effect. The paintings done in coloured glass depict stories from Jain scriptures.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Monument- Indore- Rajwada
sections.content: The Rajawada with its 7-storeyed gateway is a mixture of French, Mughal and Maratha styles. Its lofty entrance archway above a huge wooden door encrusted with iron studs, leads into a vast courtyard enclosed by galleried rooms. The lower three floors are made of stone and the upper floors are made of wood.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Monument- Mandu
sections.content: Mandu was built by the Paramara ruler Raja Bhoja and was once the capital of Malwa. It was built in the fifteenth century as a summer retreat. Jahaz Mahal is a unique monument in the shape of a ship which connects two lakes Kapur Talao and Munj Talao. Its unique construction shows the taste and the prosperous art and architecture of the past. Jahaz Mahal was built in fifteenth century when the place was under the rule of Ghiyas-ud-Din. Hindola Mahal means a swinging hall. It was built under the rule of Ghiyas-ud-din. The monument is an audience hall which is adorned with wonderful sculptures. The mahal was built with sand stone with beautifully carved columns. To the western front of the mahal there are few other mahals whose identities are not yet unveiled. Champa Baoli is a construction that stands in the midst of the Mahal depicting the past. There is a provision of hot and cold water that are also connected with the underground rooms.

sections.heading: Gwalior fort
sections.content: Gwalior is an ancient city which was under the illustrious rule of the Scindias prior to India's independence. Gwalior was once known as Gopadri or Gopachala. It has relics from the period of the Guptas, Huns, Pratiharas, Tomaras, Pathans, Moghuls, Marathas and the British. Among the temples of interest at Gwalior are the Chaturbhuj temple, the Sas Bahu temple and the Teli Ka Mandir. The Chaturbhuj temple dedicated to Vishnu is located on the eastern road to the fort. It is a rock cut monolithic structure and it was built in the year 875 during the rule of the Pratiharas. The Sas Bahu temples are located on the eastern slope of the Gopadri hill. Both of these temples, built in the Nagara style of architecture are dedicated to Padmanabha or Vishnu. Ornately decorated, the doorways, ceilings, and the

sections.heading: Sas Bahu Temple
sections.content: pillars are covered with intricate sculptural work.The hundred feet tall Teli Ka Mandir dates back to the ninth century and it is the highest building in Gwalior fort. Most of the decorative details in this temple follow the nagara idiom, while the tower is in the dravidian style.Near this temple Also in the fort is the tomb of Tansen, the musician who adorned the court of Akbar. Several Jain sculptures dating back to the fifteenth century adorn the slopes of the hill. Other attractions in the fort include the Gurjari Mahal built by Raja Mansingh during the

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Monument- Sanchi
sections.content: Sanchi, one of the most distinct archaeological sites in India is located right in the middle of the country. The world heritage site of Sanchi is being represented by various monuments including stupas, monolithic Asokan pillar, temples, monasteries and great sculptural wealth built over several centuries from the early Mauryan period to the twelfth century. It was Emperor Asoka who laid the foundations of a religious centre at Sanchi by erecting a monolithic pillar. He erected the stupa 1 here after redistribution of mortal remains of Lord Buddha for erecting several stupas all over the country in order to spread Buddhism. This stupa was originally a low structure of bricks, half the diameter of the present edifice hemispherical in shape with raised terraces at the base. It was enclosed by a wooden railing and a stone umbrella at the top. This great stupa later served as a nucleus to the large Buddhist establishment. Ashoka built a total of eight stupas on the hilltop of Sanchi including the great stupa. A number of stupas and other religious structures were added over the succeeding centuries. With the decline of Buddhism, the site decayed and was eventually completely forgotten. But, between1912 and 1919, the structures were rediscovered and carefully restored to their present condition. Originally stupas were mounds covering the relics of the Buddha or his followers. In its earliest stages Buddhist art didn't represent the Buddha directly. Instead, his presence was alluded to through symbols such as the bodhi tree, the wheel of law or his footprint. The stupa also became a symbol of the Buddha. More exactly, it became a symbol of his final release from the cycle of birth and rebirth - the Mahaparinirvana. During the Sunga period, several edifices were raised at Sanchi and its surrounding hills. The Ashoka stupa was enlarged and faced with stones and decorated with balustrades, staircases and a harmika on the top. In the Ist century BCE the Andhra-Satavahanas, whose boundaries covered the Malwa region, added the elaborately carved gateways to stupa 1 which is the most elaborate and well known of more than fifty magnificent Buddhist monuments that crown the hilltop of Sanchi. A nearly perfect hemispherical dome, the great stupa1 is topped by a triple parasol set within a square railing or harmika. A third of the way up from its base, a raised terrace, enclosed by a fence, is meant for ritual circumambulation of the monument. A second, stone-paved procession-path at ground-level is enclosed by an encircling stone balustrade. This path is accessed from the cardinal directions through four exquisitely carved gateways. The exquisite carvings of the doorway depict in detail the significant episodes and miracles from Lord Buddhas life and events depicted in the Buddhist jataka stories. The eastern gateway depicts the young prince, Gautama leaving his father's palace on his journey towards enlightenment and the dream his mother had before his birth. The western gateway depicts the seven incarnations of the Buddha. The northern gateway crowned by a wheel-of-law, this depicts the miracles associated with the Buddha as told in the Jatakas. The southern gateway shows the birth of Gautama revealed in a series of dramatically rich carvings. From the second to fourth century CE Sanchi and Vidisha came under the rule of Kushanas and Kshatrapas and subsequently passed on to the hands of the Guptas. During the Gupta period some temples were also built and sculptures were added displaying the classical grace and simplicity of the era. Further, statues of Lord Buddha seated in the canopies facing the four entrances of the great Stupa were also added. Sanchi also flourished during the seventh century when shrines and monasteries were continued to be added. Thus Sanchi displays harmonious co-existence of Hindu and Buddhist faiths.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Handicrafts Stonecraft
sections.content: Balaghat has a lovely green stone out of which the local carvers make a number of small items, animals, boxes, trays, etc. But the important products are the religious images.

sections.heading: Papier-mache Craft
sections.content: Madhya Pradesh is well known for papier-mâché items. The main center for papier-mâché is Ujjain but this craft is also popular in Gwalior, Ratlam and Bhopal. Craftsmen from Gwalior and Bhopal make statues of birds, animals and decorative panels. The craftsmen of Ujjain make papier-mâché birds and figures of popular deities. These products

sections.heading: Jewellery
sections.content: Madhya Pradesh makes lac jewellery, the best known being in Rewa and Indore. In these places ornaments like chokers, earrings, rings, hair ornaments and large octagonal bead chains are made in traditional style. In this type of jewellery, lac is placed over the tin foil and melted so that the latter is fully covered by lac. This is largely used for ornaments which shine with a golden effect. One of the most attractive pieces made by this process is the anklet of clove shaped beads all cast in one piece called lauang kasauthi.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Handicrafts -Toy Making
sections.content: The tradition of making a special type of traditional rag dolls is prevalent in Gwalior.The faces of these dolls are painted beautifully and the eyes are painted in such a manner that they give them a very lively expression. The dolls are dressed in paper costumes in traditional style. The dolls are highly decorated and ornamented. These dolls are popularly known as battubai dolls as they were created by a woman named Battubai.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Handicrafts -Maheshwari Sarees
sections.content: The Maheshwari saree in Madhya Pradesh has an unusual origin for it is traced to a generous queen who once ruled over that territory and designed the first saree. Maheshwar, the place itself is a charming one on the banks of the river Narmada. The Maheshwari saree, mostly in cotton is characterised by its simplicity . The body is either plain or has stripes or checks with several variations. A speciality of the Maheshwari saree is its reversible border because of which either side of the saree can be worn. This is locally known as bugdi. The borders have a wide range of mat designs which consists of floral designs, the best known amongst which is the karanphool pattern.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Handicrafts- Bandhani
sections.content: Madhya Pradesh has very unusual and attractive bandhanis or tie and dye work. The best known centres are two villages in western Madhya Pradesh on the opposite banks of river Gujari known as Tarapur and Umedpura. Mandsaur also produces some excellent bandhani. Amongst the wide selection of designs the most common is of chains of grains represented by dots on the body called the dana pattern while there are elaborate designs on the borders and pallus.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Handicarfts-Printed Textiles
sections.content: The Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh has long being known for its printed cotton textiles which are printed in different techniques like direct dyeing and printing, resist dyeing and printing, rogan printing and screen printing. The important centres are Jawad, Bhairongarh, Tarapur, Umedpura and Sheopur. The communities engaged in this craft are chippa, rangrez and nilgar. Jawad was once famous for exporting the reknowned jazams to various countries under royal patronage.

sections.heading: Madhya Pradesh- Handicrafts-Durries
sections.content: The durries of Madhya Pradesh, from Jobat and Tipgaon in the tribal district of Jhabua are well known for their sturdy character and delightful colours. Weaving in Jobat is simple, done on the pitlooms with panja, a woodden apparatus, almost like an extension of the hand, used to pull back firmly and fix the weft yarn in place. These mats are very attractive because of their delightful warm tints.

sections.heading: Fresco is a technique where the painting is done when the plaster on the wall is still wet therefore the colors intermingle permanently with the plaster and is permanent.
sections.content: Mural painting refers to paintings on walls, ceilings, or other large permanent surfaces. This style of painting can be traced back to prehistoric times such as the paintings on the Caves of Lascaux in southern France. The term Mural came into being with the Mexican muralista art movement. Fresco is a technique where the painting is done when the plaster on the wall is still wet therefore the colors intermingle permanently with the plaster and is permanent. For quite some time the art work was mistakenly referred to as "frescoes". We now know that the proper term for this kind of artwork is known as mural because the known process and technique of fresco painting isn't found in this kind of art. At Ajanta, the technique and process used to produce this kind of artwork is unlike any other artwork found in the art history of other civilizations. These murals have a uniqueness about them. The process of painting involved several stages. The first step was to chisel the rock surface, to make it rough enough to hold the plaster. The plaster was made of clay, hay, cowdung and lime. Differences are found in the ingredients and their proportions from cave to cave. While the plaster was still wet, the drawings were done and the colors applied. The wet plaster had the capacity to soak the color so that the color became a part of the surface and would not peel off or decay easily. The colors were referred to as 'earth colors' or 'vegetable colors.' Various kinds of stones, minerals, and plants were used in combinations to prepare different colors. Sculptures were often covered with stucco to give them a fine finish and lustrous polish. The stucco had the ingredients of lime and powdered sea-shell or conch. The latter afforded exceptional shine and smoothness. In cave upper six, some of it is extant. The smoothness resembles the surface of glass. The paint brushes used to create the artwork were made from animal hair and twigs.
